title: Circular and rotational motion
summary: Learn why a turning object is accelerating. Explore curves, vertical circles, and angular momentum.
cards.0.p: If an object on a circle covers equal distances in equal times, it is in uniform circular motion. Its speed is constant, but its velocity is always tangent and keeps changing direction. So the object is accelerating.
cards.0.key: The speed is constant, but the velocity vector changes. That is why uniform circular motion is accelerated motion.
cards.1.p: The time for one turn is the period (T). The number of turns per second is the frequency (f). f = 1/T, and frequency is measured in hertz (1/s).
cards.1.svg#2: T: the time for one turn
cards.1.key: For a drum spinning at 1200 turns per minute, f = 20 Hz and T = 0.05 s. The longer the period, the lower the frequency.
cards.2.p: In one turn the object travels 2πr, so v = 2πr/T. The angular speed is ω = 2π/T (rad/s). The two are linked by v = ω·r.
cards.2.key: On a Ferris wheel every point has the same angular speed, but the linear speed grows with the radius. One turn equals 2π rad, or 360°.
cards.3.p: The acceleration that changes the direction of the velocity always points toward the center, and a = v²/r = ω²·r. It is perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes only the direction, not the speed.
cards.3.key: If v = 10 m/s and r = 20 m, then a = 100/20 = 5 m/s².
cards.3.once.soru: If you take the same curve twice as fast, how many times larger is the centripetal acceleration?
cards.3.once.secenekler.0.neden: Since a = v²/r, the acceleration grows with the square of the speed: 2² = 4 times.
cards.3.once.secenekler.1.neden: The acceleration grows with the square of the speed, not with the speed.
cards.3.once.secenekler.2.neden: The radius stayed the same, but the speed went up. The acceleration depends on the speed.
cards.4.h: Centripetal force is not a new force
cards.4.p: Centripetal acceleration needs a net force toward the center, and that force is F = m·v²/r. Forces you already know supply it: tension, friction, or gravity.
cards.4.svg#9: all toward the center: Fnet = m·v²/r
cards.4.key: For a whirling stone it is the string tension, for a car on a curve it is friction, and for the Moon it is Earth's gravity. Don't draw a separate centripetal force arrow on a free-body diagram. Centripetal force is a name for the net force.
cards.5.h: A car on a curve: friction
cards.5.p: On a level road, the force that turns a car through a curve is static friction. So the maximum safe speed is v = √(μs·g·r), and it does not depend on mass.
cards.5.key: Friction can be at most μs·m·g. If μs = 0.8 and r = 80 m, then v ≈ 25 m/s. On a wet or icy road μs is smaller, and so is the safe speed.
cards.5.etk.soru: Change the road's coefficient of friction and the radius of the curve. Dry asphalt μ ≈ 0.7, wet ≈ 0.4, ice ≈ 0.1.
cards.6.p: On a banked curve, the horizontal component of the normal force points toward the center. So even without friction you can turn safely at one particular speed. That speed comes from tanθ = v²/(r·g).
cards.6.key: That is why racetracks and highway curves tilt inward. With friction as well, the range of safe speeds gets wider.
cards.6.once.soru: Why are the curves on racetracks tilted inward?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.yazi: So the road pushes the car toward the center
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The normal force of a tilted road points partly toward the center. So friction has less work to do.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: The tilt does drain water, but the main purpose is to make turning easier.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: The opposite. The tilt lets cars take the curve faster.
cards.7.p: When an object on a string moves in a horizontal circle, the string makes an angle α with the vertical. The vertical component of the tension balances the weight, and the horizontal component supplies the centripetal force. So tanα = v²/(r·g).
cards.7.key: T·cosα = m·g and T·sinα = m·v²/r. The faster the object, the closer the string gets to horizontal.
cards.7.once.soru: You tie a stone to a string and whirl it horizontally above your head. Can the string be exactly horizontal?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: Balancing the weight takes an upward component of the tension. So the string always slopes down a little.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.yazi: Yes, if you whirl it fast
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: The faster it goes, the closer the string gets to horizontal. But because of the weight, it never gets exactly there.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: When you whirl it slowly, the string clearly hangs downward.
cards.8.h: Vertical circle: minimum speed at the top
cards.8.p: At the top of a vertical circle, the weight and the tension both point toward the center, so W + T = m·v²/r. At the limit T = 0, this gives v = √(g·r). If the object is slower than that, the string goes slack.
cards.8.key: At the bottom, T − W = m·v²/r. In a roller coaster loop, the rider does not fall if v ≥ √(g·r) at the top.
cards.8.once.soru: You whirl a stone on a string in a vertical circle. Where is the string pulled tightest?
cards.8.once.secenekler.0.neden: At the bottom, the tension has to both overcome the weight and supply the centripetal force.
cards.8.once.secenekler.1.neden: At the top, the weight does part of the job. So the tension is smallest there.
cards.8.once.secenekler.2.neden: The weight always points down. So the tension changes with position.
cards.9.p: When a car turns, you feel pushed against the door. In fact your body keeps going straight because of inertia, and the door pushes you toward the center. No real force pushes you outward.
cards.9.key: “Centrifugal” is only an inertia effect felt by the turning observer. For an observer on the ground, there is only a net force toward the center.
cards.9.once.soru: When a car turns left, what presses you against the door on the right?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Your body wants to go straight. The car turns underneath you, and the door pushes you toward the center.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: No real force pushes you outward. It is only a feeling.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Friction from the seat tries to turn you with the car. It does not push you outward.
cards.10.p: The measure of resistance to rotation is called the moment of inertia: I = Σm·r². The farther the mass is spread from the axis, the larger I is. For a ring I = M·R², and for a solid disk it is ½·M·R².
cards.10.svg#0: same mass M, same radius R
cards.10.key: I depends not only on the mass but also on how far the mass is from the axis of rotation.
cards.10.once.soru: A ring and a solid disk have the same mass and radius. Which one is harder to start spinning?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: All of the ring's mass is far from the axis. So it resists rotation more.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Part of the disk's mass is close to the axis. So it resists less.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The mass is the same, but it is spread differently. Resistance to rotation depends on how the mass is spread.
cards.11.p: The angular momentum of a rotating object is L = I·ω. With no external torque, angular momentum is conserved, so I1·ω1 = I2·ω2. For a point object, L = m·r·v⊥.
cards.11.key: When a planet gets closer to the Sun, r gets smaller and v gets larger. A diver doing a somersault tucks in to make I smaller and spins faster.
cards.12.p: The kinetic energy of a rotating object is ½·I·ω². When an object rolls without slipping, its energy is shared between moving forward and rotating. So it comes down more slowly than a box sliding without friction.
cards.12.svg#0: bottom speed from the same height h (× √(g·h))
cards.12.svg#9: the box slides without friction, the others roll without slipping
cards.12.key: In rolling, v = ω·r and the total energy is ½·m·v² + ½·I·ω².
cards.12.once.soru: A solid cylinder and a thin ring roll down the same ramp at the same moment. Which one gets down first?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: The cylinder has a smaller I. Less of its energy goes into rotation, so it moves forward faster.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: The ring has a large I. Most of its energy goes into rotation, so it moves forward slowly.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: Their mass is spread differently. So they share the energy differently.
cards.13.p:
• The speed is constant, the direction of the velocity changes, and f = 1/T.
• Linear speed is v = ω·r = 2πr/T.
• F = m·v²/r is not a new force. It is the net force toward the center.
• On a curve v ≤ √(μ·g·r), and at the top of a vertical circle v ≥ √(g·r).
• With no external torque, L = I·ω is conserved.
quiz.0.q: With arms out, a skater has a moment of inertia of 3 kg·m² and spins at 2 turns per second. Pulling the arms in lowers the moment of inertia to 1.2 kg·m². How many turns per second does the skater make now? (no external torque)
quiz.0.e: Angular momentum is conserved, so I<sub>1</sub>·f<sub>1</sub> = I<sub>2</sub>·f<sub>2</sub>. Since 3·2 = 1.2·f<sub>2</sub>, f<sub>2</sub> = 5 turns/s.
quiz.1.q: For an object in uniform circular motion, put each quantity in the right group.
quiz.1.e: Since the speed is constant, so are the period, ω, and ½·m·v². The velocity is always tangent, and the acceleration and net force always point toward the center, so the direction of these three changes at every moment.
quiz.2.q: Which force supplies the centripetal force in each case? Match them.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.0: A stone whirled on a string
quiz.2.ciftler.1.0: A car turning on a level curve
quiz.2.ciftler.3.0: A car on a frictionless banked curve
quiz.2.ciftler.3.1: Horizontal component of the normal force
quiz.2.e: Centripetal force is not a new force. For the stone it is the string tension, on a level curve it is static friction, and for the Moon it is gravity. On a banked curve it is the horizontal component of the normal force, which points toward the center.
quiz.3.q: A vertical loop at an amusement park has a radius of 10 m. What minimum speed, in m/s, does the car need at the top to keep pressing on the track? (g = 10 m/s²)
quiz.3.e: At the top, in the limiting case, the weight alone supplies the centripetal force, so m·g = m·v²/r. That gives v = √(g·r) = √(10·10) = 10 m/s.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Watch the ball go around, compare speeds on a Ferris wheel, and take a curve without skidding.
A:adimlar.0.metin: The ball goes around the circle at constant speed. The velocity arrow is always tangent to the circle, and since its direction changes, the ball is accelerating.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which way does this acceleration point?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A tangent acceleration would change the speed. But the speed is constant.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: An acceleration that changes only the direction, not the speed, is perpendicular to the velocity and always points toward the center (red arrow). It is called centripetal acceleration.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: An outward acceleration would move the ball away from the circle. Which way must the acceleration point to bend the ball's path around the circle?
A:adimlar.1.metin: Frequency is the number of turns per second, measured in hertz. Set the washing machine drum to 25 Hz.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 1500 turns per minute is 1500 / 60 = 25 turns per second, so f = 25 Hz. One turn takes T = 1/25 = 0.04 s.
A:adimlar.2.metin: The Ferris wheel makes one turn every 20 seconds. You are in the outer seat, 8 m from the center. Your friend is in the inner seat, 4 m from the center.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: We move at the same speed
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: You both go around in the same time, so your angular speed is the same. But the outer seat covers more distance.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In one turn the outer seat travels 2π·8 ≈ 50 m and the inner seat about 25 m, and both do it in 20 s. Twice the distance in the same time means twice the speed.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The seat near the center traces a smaller circle and covers less distance in the same time.
A:adimlar.3.metin: You whirl a stone on a string in a horizontal plane, and we are looking from above. The string will break when the stone is at its northernmost point, moving east.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: Where does the stone go when the string breaks?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Once the force pulling toward the center is gone, the first law says the stone keeps the velocity it has and moves straight along the tangent. A hammer thrower lets go at exactly this kind of moment.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: No force pushes outward. Centrifugal force is a misconception.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The string tension was what kept the stone on the circle. Without it, the path becomes straight.
A:adimlar.4.metin: The centripetal force needed is F = m·v²/r. A 1000 kg car is on a curve with a radius of 50 m. Change the speed and make the force 8000 N.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: 1000 · 20² / 50 = 8000 N. When the speed doubles from 10 m/s to 20 m/s, the force needed becomes four times larger. This is not a new force. Here, friction between the tires and the road supplies it.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The maximum safe speed on a curve is √(μ·g·r), where μ is the surface's coefficient of friction. Your car will take a 50 m curve at 15 m/s. Choose the road surface and take the curve without skidding.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: At μ = 0.5 the limit is √(0.5 · 9.8 · 50) ≈ 15.7 m/s, so 15 m/s is safe. In rain μ drops, and so does the limit. That is why you slow down on a wet road.
A:adimlar.6.metin: A skater spins with arms out, and there is no external torque. Pulling the arms in to the body will cut the moment of inertia I in half.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: What happens when the skater pulls the arms in?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: If I gets smaller while L stays constant, ω must get larger.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: The skater spins twice as fast
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The product I·ω, the angular momentum, stays constant: 4 · 2 = 2 · 4. When I is cut in half, ω doubles.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: If the spin stayed the same, cutting I in half would cut L in half too. But L cannot change without an external torque.
A:kapanis.0: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant, but the direction of the velocity changes. So the object is accelerating, and the acceleration always points toward the center.
A:kapanis.1: f = 1/T and v = ω·r = 2πr/T. On a rotating object ω is the same at every point, while v grows with the radius.
A:kapanis.2: F = m·v²/r is not a new force. It is the net force toward the center. Tension, friction, or gravity supplies it.
A:kapanis.3: When the force is gone, the object moves straight along the tangent. On a level curve the safe speed is v ≤ √(μ·g·r).
A:kapanis.4: With no external torque, angular momentum L = I·ω is conserved.
